title: European Power Rivalry
summary: German unification in 1871 transformed Europe's balance of power. The new German Empire became the strongest continental state, while France sought security after defeat, Austria-Hungary and Russia competed in the Balkans, and Britain watched Germany's industrial and naval growth. Rivalry did not make war inevitable, but it made later crises harder to contain.

title: Franco-German Rivalry after 1871
summary: France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War and Germany's annexation of Alsace-Lorraine left a durable grievance after 1871. Recovery of the provinces remained a powerful symbol in France, although French diplomacy also pursued broader security, colonial, and balance-of-power aims. The rivalry encouraged France to seek partners against diplomatic isolation.

title: Pan-Slavic Solidarity
summary: Pan-Slavic ideas promoted cultural and political solidarity among Slavic peoples, but Russian policy toward Serbia also reflected strategy, prestige, and competition with Austria-Hungary. The language of Slavic protection made withdrawal from Balkan crises politically costly without mechanically determining Russian decisions.

title: Balkan Rivalry
summary: The Congress of Berlin in 1878 revised the settlement of the Russo-Turkish War and expanded Austro-Hungarian influence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Russia and Austria-Hungary increasingly competed over influence as Ottoman power receded, while Balkan states pursued their own ambitions. This rivalry repeatedly linked local disputes to Great-Power prestige.

title: Rival Alliance Blocs
summary: European powers formed alliances to deter attack and avoid isolation. The agreements were not one automatic chain: obligations were conditional, Italy stayed neutral in 1914, and Britain had no treaty duty to fight for France or Russia. During the July Crisis, however, uncertainty about allies and fear of abandonment encouraged risky reassurance and made coalition warfare easier once leaders chose escalation.

title: Dual and Triple Alliances
summary: Germany and Austria-Hungary formed the Dual Alliance in 1879, and Italy joined them in the Triple Alliance in 1882. The treaties were defensive and their members did not interpret every crisis alike; Italy declared neutrality in 1914 and joined the opposing coalition in 1915. The durable Berlin-Vienna partnership nevertheless provided the political setting for Germany's exceptional support of Austria-Hungary in July 1914.

title: Franco-Russian Alliance
summary: France and Russia developed a military alliance in the early 1890s to counter the strategic position of Germany and its allies. Its conventions linked a German mobilisation or attack against one partner to preparations by the other, making a two-front war central to German planning. Political leaders still retained choices during a crisis, but abandoning the alliance carried major strategic costs.

title: Entente Cordiale
summary: The Entente Cordiale of 1904 settled colonial disputes between Britain and France, especially over Egypt and Morocco. It was not a military alliance, yet subsequent crises and staff conversations produced growing strategic cooperation. By 1914 Britain remained legally free to stay neutral, but a German defeat of France threatened British security and the Channel coast.

title: Anglo-Russian Entente
summary: Britain and Russia settled several imperial disputes in 1907, completing the diplomatic alignment later called the Triple Entente. The agreement was not an alliance requiring British intervention, and Anglo-Russian suspicion persisted. It nevertheless reduced Britain's isolation and contributed to the perception of two rival European blocs.

title: European Arms Race Accelerates
summary: The Anglo-German naval competition had begun before HMS Dreadnought appeared in 1906, particularly with Germany's Naval Laws from 1898. Dreadnought accelerated the contest by resetting battleship standards, while continental powers enlarged armies, improved railways, and expanded artillery. The buildup heightened insecurity and strengthened military assumptions, but weapons themselves did not force governments to use them.

title: German Two-Front War Planning
summary: German planners expected that a war involving Russia would probably also involve France. Schlieffen's 1905 memorandum and the deployment plan used by Moltke in 1914 concentrated most German forces in the west, violated Belgian neutrality, and sought a rapid decision before shifting strength east. The postwar claim that Moltke merely ruined a flawless plan by weakening its right wing is disputed; the strategy faced severe logistical and political risks from the start.

title: Mobilization Timetables
summary: Mass armies required elaborate railway schedules, reserve call-ups, and supply plans. Mobilisation was not literally irreversible or identical to a declaration of war, but leaders feared that delay would surrender a decisive operational advantage. Timetables narrowed perceived options and gave generals increasing influence as the July Crisis escalated.

title: Bosnian Annexation Crisis
summary: Austria-Hungary formally annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1908 after administering it since 1878. Serbia protested, and Russia—militarily weakened and expecting diplomatic compensation from Vienna—ultimately backed down under German pressure. The episode deepened Serbian hostility, Russian resentment, and Vienna's confidence that pressure could isolate Belgrade.

title: Serbian Nationalism
summary: Serbian political and cultural movements promoted the unification of Serbs and, in some versions, a wider South Slav state. These ambitions overlapped with but were not identical to the aims of every Bosnian revolutionary. Vienna regarded Serbian influence among Habsburg South Slavs as a serious threat to imperial cohesion.

title: Black Hand
summary: The Black Hand, formally Union or Death, was a conspiratorial Serbian officers' organisation founded in 1911. Networks linked to its leader Dragutin Dimitrijević, head of Serbian military intelligence, helped arm and move the Young Bosnia conspirators across the border. The plot was not authorised by Serbia's civilian government, although officials may have received fragmentary warnings.

title: Balkan Wars
summary: In the First Balkan War, Serbia, Bulgaria, Greece, and Montenegro removed most remaining Ottoman rule from Europe; in the second, the former allies fought over the settlement. Serbia emerged larger and more confident but was blocked from an Adriatic outlet. Its growth intensified Austro-Hungarian fears and sharpened regional rivalry.

title: Vienna Fears Serbian Expansion
summary: A larger Serbia promoting South Slav unity appeared dangerous to leaders of the multi-national Habsburg monarchy. Vienna feared that Serbian prestige and covert activism would encourage separatism among imperial Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. This was a powerful perception rather than proof that collapse was inevitable, and Habsburg officials disagreed over whether reform, pressure, or war offered the best response.

title: Assassination of Franz Ferdinand
summary: On 28 June 1914, Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb member of Young Bosnia, shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in Sarajevo. Black Hand-linked officers had helped arm and train the conspirators, but the Serbian civilian government did not sanction the operation. After an earlier bomb failed, a routing mistake brought the royal car to a stop near Princip; the killings opened a crisis whose escalation still depended on political choices.

title: Vienna Chooses a Reckoning
summary: Several Austro-Hungarian leaders had long wanted a decisive reckoning with Serbia, while others urged caution. The assassination created an opportunity to weaken Serbian influence and restore Habsburg prestige. Because a local war might bring Russian intervention, Vienna first sought firm support from Berlin.

title: German Blank Cheque
summary: On 5–6 July 1914, Germany assured Austria-Hungary of full support even if action against Serbia produced war with Russia. The 'blank cheque' removed a major restraint on Vienna and encouraged a deliberately severe course. Historians continue to debate German motives, but the assurance was one of the most consequential decisions of the July Crisis.

title: Austrian Ultimatum
summary: Austria-Hungary delivered a forty-eight-hour ultimatum to Serbia on 23 July. Its demands required suppression of anti-Habsburg activity and Austro-Hungarian participation in investigations inside Serbia; Vienna had framed the note so that refusal, and therefore military action, was highly likely. The timing and severity limited mediation after weeks in which Austria-Hungary and Germany had concealed their intentions.

title: Serbia Gives a Qualified Acceptance
summary: Serbia accepted many demands, accepted others with qualifications, and rejected or referred to international arbitration the provisions that would give Austro-Hungarian officials authority inside Serbia. The reply appeared conciliatory to other powers, but Vienna had already decided that a merely diplomatic success was insufficient. Diplomatic relations were broken off shortly after the deadline.

title: Austria-Hungary Attacks Serbia
summary: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914 and soon bombarded Belgrade. The declaration began the local war Vienna had planned, but it did not automatically activate every alliance. It intensified Russian military preparations and triggered a new round of mobilisation, ultimatums, and failed mediation.

title: Russia Backs Serbia
summary: Russia regarded the destruction of Serbia as a blow to its Balkan influence and Great-Power status. On 25 July it authorised preparatory military measures, implemented from 26 July, while also supporting mediation. After Austria-Hungary declared war, Russian leaders moved from preparations toward mobilisation despite disagreement between the Tsar, ministers, and generals.

title: Russian General Mobilization
summary: Russia ordered general mobilisation on 30 July after an unstable attempt to mobilise only against Austria-Hungary. Mobilisation was not a formal declaration of war, but German leaders treated it as an immediate strategic threat and issued an ultimatum demanding reversal. Russian planners argued that partial mobilisation would disrupt the railway system and leave the army dangerously exposed.

title: Germany Declares War on Russia
summary: Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August 1914 after its ultimatum demanding demobilisation expired. The decision converted the Austro-Serbian war into a direct conflict between Great Powers. German mobilisation and two-front planning then accelerated the attack in the west.

title: France Stands with Russia
summary: France reassured Russia during the crisis because the alliance was central to French security against Germany. Paris nevertheless tried to avoid appearing the aggressor, delaying some measures and withdrawing troops from the frontier. France ordered general mobilisation on 1 August as war between Germany and Russia began.

title: Germany Declares War on France
summary: Germany declared war on France on 3 August 1914, alleging hostile acts while implementing its western deployment plan. France's alliance with Russia made its participation highly likely, but the German decision determined the form and timing of the western war. German forces were already preparing to advance through Luxembourg and Belgium.

title: Invasion of Belgium
summary: Germany invaded Belgium on 4 August after Belgium rejected a demand for free passage. The attack violated Belgian neutrality guaranteed in the 1839 settlement and placed German forces near the Channel coast. Belgium was not Britain's only concern, but the invasion supplied the decisive legal, strategic, and moral case that united most of the British cabinet and public behind intervention.

title: British Security and Balance Concerns
summary: British leaders feared that a German victory over France and control of the Channel coast would threaten national security, sea communications, and the European balance of power. Cooperation with France had grown, but Britain had no automatic obligation under the Ententes. The cabinet remained divided until the invasion of Belgium transformed the political calculation.

title: Britain Enters War
summary: Britain issued an ultimatum demanding respect for Belgian neutrality and declared war on Germany at 11 p.m. on 4 August 1914. Strategic concern about German domination of western Europe mattered alongside treaty and moral arguments about Belgium. The declaration applied across the British Empire, while self-governing Dominions determined how extensively they would mobilise.

title: European War Begins
summary: Between 28 July and 4 August 1914, a planned Austro-Serbian war expanded into a European conflict through successive choices in Vienna, Berlin, St. Petersburg, Paris, and London. The assassination supplied the trigger, but war was not an automatic product of alliances or timetables. Leaders accepted escalating risks amid nationalism, military planning, imperial rivalry, and fear of losing status or allies.

title: War Becomes Global
summary: The conflict became global because the belligerents were empires with worldwide armies, colonies, sea lanes, and commercial networks. Britain and its empire, Japan, the Ottoman Empire, and later Italy, Bulgaria, Romania, and the United States widened the theatres of war. Fighting and wartime extraction affected Europe, Africa, Asia, the Middle East, the Pacific, and the world's oceans.

title: The Western Front Entrenches
summary: Germany's advance was stopped at the Marne in September 1914, after which both sides attempted to outflank one another northward. By late autumn a continuous fortified front stretched from the Channel to Switzerland. Firepower, field fortification, manpower, and logistics made defence powerful; the Western Front remained largely positional until 1918, although major offensives repeatedly shifted parts of the line.

title: Gallipoli Campaign
summary: The Allied attempt to force the Dardanelles began with naval attacks in February–March 1915 and landings on the Gallipoli peninsula in April. Ottoman resistance contained the bridgeheads, and trench warfare, disease, and repeated failed offensives produced more than half a million casualties across both sides before the Allies evacuated in December 1915 and January 1916. It was an Ottoman victory and a formative event in Turkish, Australian, and New Zealand memory—not a step that directly caused Ottoman defeat.

title: Battle of the Somme
summary: The Somme offensive of July–November 1916 was planned jointly by Britain and France and became more urgent as France fought at Verdun. It failed to achieve the expected breakthrough and cost more than one million killed, wounded, or captured, while the British advanced at most about eleven kilometres. Yet it relieved pressure on France, inflicted severe losses on Germany, and accelerated tactical learning, making it more than a battle for negligible ground alone.

title: Industrial War of Attrition
summary: Industrial war became a contest of manpower, production, finance, food, transport, and political endurance. Blockade, artillery, repeated offensives, occupation, disease, and requisitioning harmed soldiers and civilians across multiple fronts. Attrition did not affect all states equally, and military outcomes still depended on strategy and coalition resources.

title: Imperial and Colonial Mobilization
summary: European empires mobilised millions of soldiers, labourers, and carriers from outside Europe. About 1.5 million officers and men served in the British Indian Army, while France and Britain drew extensively on African, Asian, Caribbean, and Pacific populations; recruitment included both volunteering and coercion. Wartime service reshaped claims to citizenship and independence, but anti-colonial movements had deeper roots and developed differently after the war.

title: United States Enters War
summary: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February 1917, accepting the risk of American intervention in an attempt to defeat Britain quickly. The Zimmermann Telegram, proposing an alliance with Mexico if war came, further inflamed U.S. opinion. Congress declared war on Germany on 6 April; American finance, supplies, naval power, and eventually more than two million soldiers in Europe strengthened the Allies, although U.S. troops were one part of the wider German defeat.

title: Russian Revolution
summary: Military losses, food and transport breakdowns, inflation, labour unrest, and the Tsarist regime's political failures helped produce the February Revolution of 1917 and Nicholas II's abdication. The Provisional Government continued the war and lost authority; the Bolsheviks seized power in October promising peace, land, and bread. War was a central catalyst, not the sole cause of Russia's revolutions.

title: Home Front Pressure
summary: Total war strained food supplies, state finances, labour relations, and political legitimacy. Blockades, inflation, casualties, requisitioning, and unequal sacrifice generated strikes, mutinies, protests, and national movements in different combinations across the belligerents. These pressures weakened Russia, Austria-Hungary, Germany, and the Ottoman Empire but did not produce identical outcomes everywhere.

title: Russia Exits the War
summary: The Bolshevik government agreed an armistice in December 1917 and signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918, abandoning vast western territories and recognising several separations under Central Powers pressure. Germany transferred large forces west for the Spring Offensive. Russia's exit gave Germany a temporary advantage, but the failed offensive exhausted men and supplies before American strength fully arrived.

title: Ottoman Defeat and Armistice
summary: Ottoman defeat resulted from prolonged campaigns, enormous casualties, desertion, shortages, disease, and Allied advances in Palestine, Syria, and Mesopotamia. The empire had won at Gallipoli and retained some cohesive formations, but by autumn 1918 Bulgaria's surrender exposed Constantinople while Allenby's forces broke the southern front. The Armistice of Mudros on 30 October ended Ottoman participation without immediately determining the empire's final borders.

title: German Military Collapse
summary: Germany's Spring Offensive failed after costly initial gains, and the Allied Hundred Days then drove German armies backward from August 1918. American manpower and material, Allied combined-arms adaptation, blockade, shortages, influenza, collapsing allies, and declining morale all contributed. The army was not annihilated, but its commanders told the government that victory was impossible; revolution and the Kiel mutiny followed, and Wilhelm II left power on 9 November.

title: Armistice Ends the Fighting
summary: The armistice signed at Compiègne stopped fighting on the Western Front at 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918. Estimates vary, but roughly sixteen million or more soldiers and civilians had died, with many additional deaths from famine, displacement, and disease. The armistice ended combat with Germany; it was not itself a peace treaty and did not make the later political settlement or another world war inevitable.

title: Treaty of Versailles
summary: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in June 1919 after negotiations from which Germany was excluded until presented with the draft. Germany lost its colonies and about 13 percent of its European territory, accepted military restrictions, and became liable for reparations; the 132-billion-gold-mark figure was fixed in 1921, not in the treaty itself. Article 231 established legal responsibility for war damage and was denounced in Germany as a moral 'war guilt clause,' becoming a potent political grievance.

title: Ottoman Empire Enters the War
summary: The Ottoman government concluded a secret alliance with Germany in August 1914 and entered the war after Ottoman ships attacked Russian ports in the Black Sea in late October. Its intervention opened or intensified fronts in the Caucasus, Dardanelles, Mesopotamia, Sinai-Palestine, and Arabia. Allied plans for Ottoman territory developed during the war, but the eventual settlement also reflected local actors, wartime promises, and the Turkish nationalist victory.

title: Armenian Genocide
summary: Under cover of the war, the Committee of Union and Progress government ordered the mass deportation and destruction of Ottoman Armenians. From spring 1915 through 1916, at least 664,000 and possibly as many as 1.2 million people died through massacre, forced marches, starvation, exposure, and disease; children were also abducted and forcibly assimilated. Wartime security claims supplied a pretext, but deportations expanded far beyond combat zones and formed a state-directed campaign of annihilation.

title: Arab Revolt
summary: Sharif Hussein of Mecca launched the Arab Revolt in June 1916 with British support, seeking Hashemite rule and greater independence from Ottoman centralisation. The revolt was not a universal uprising of Ottoman Arabs: many remained loyal, neutral, or followed local interests. Hashemite forces captured Red Sea ports, disrupted the Hejaz Railway, and later supported Allenby's advance while tying down Ottoman troops.

title: Allenby's Palestine Campaign
summary: Edmund Allenby's Egyptian Expeditionary Force captured Jerusalem in December 1917 and achieved a decisive breakthrough at Megiddo in September 1918. British imperial forces, including large Indian contingents, advanced through Palestine and Syria while Arab forces disrupted communications and entered Damascus. The campaign broke the Ottoman southern armies, but Ottoman defeat also reflected crises on other fronts and at home.

title: Combined Arms Breaks the Deadlock
summary: The deadlock was not broken by one wonder weapon. Gas, tanks, aircraft, improved artillery, wireless communications, sound ranging, and light machine guns mattered when integrated with intelligence, logistics, decentralised infantry tactics, and carefully coordinated fire. By 1918 the Allies applied combined-arms methods during the Hundred Days, while German exhaustion and shrinking reserves made sustained recovery increasingly difficult.

title: Italy Switches to the Allies
summary: Italy declared neutrality in 1914 because the Triple Alliance was defensive and Rome argued that Austria-Hungary had acted aggressively. The secret Treaty of London promised territory if Italy joined the Entente, and Italy entered the war against Austria-Hungary in May 1915. The Italian front imposed heavy costs on both states; the decisive Allied victory at Vittorio Veneto came only as the Habsburg state was already disintegrating.

title: Austria-Hungary Disintegrates
summary: Austria-Hungary disintegrated in October–November 1918 under military defeat, hunger, war exhaustion, and competing national movements. Czech, South Slav, Polish, German-Austrian, and Hungarian authorities asserted sovereignty as imperial institutions lost control. Emperor Karl renounced participation in government—he did not formally abdicate—and the monarchy's former territories were divided among several successor states.

title: Peace Treaties Redraw Central Europe
summary: The Treaties of Saint-Germain with Austria in 1919 and Trianon with Hungary in 1920 recognised and fixed much of the Habsburg monarchy's already accomplished dissolution. Hungary lost about two-thirds of its former territory and population, leaving large Magyar minorities outside its borders; other successor states also contained substantial minorities. The settlements stabilised some claims while generating new disputes, rather than simply replacing an ethnically mixed empire with homogeneous nation-states.

title: Sèvres Fails; Lausanne Replaces It
summary: The 1920 Treaty of Sèvres proposed severe restrictions on the Ottoman state, Greek and Armenian territorial gains, and Allied zones of influence. Turkish nationalists led by Mustafa Kemal rejected it and won the war that followed, so most of Sèvres was never implemented. The Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 recognised the borders of the new Turkish state, while separate mandate arrangements and wartime agreements shaped former Arab provinces.

title: Weimar Republic Founded
summary: Germany became a parliamentary republic amid military defeat and revolution in November 1918. The Weimar constitution created a broad democratic system, but the new state faced political violence, contested legitimacy, the Versailles settlement, fiscal strain, and the military's false 'stab-in-the-back' narrative. Democracy nevertheless gained substantial support and survived several crises before the Great Depression transformed the political environment.

title: Nazis Exploit the Postwar Crisis
summary: The Nazis exploited resentment over defeat and Versailles, antisemitism, fear of communism, and hostility to parliamentary government. Their national breakthrough came after the Great Depression produced mass unemployment and political deadlock; conservative elites then helped place Hitler in office in January 1933. The First World War and its settlement created important conditions, but Nazi rule was neither a direct nor inevitable consequence of Sarajevo.

title: League of Nations Founded
summary: The League of Nations began work in 1920 as an experiment in collective security, international administration, and cooperation. The United States never joined, and the organisation depended on member governments that were unwilling or unable to enforce sanctions against major aggressors. It achieved useful humanitarian and technical work but failed to prevent expansion by Japan, Italy, and Nazi Germany.

title: Empires Fall, Borders Shift
summary: By the early 1920s, the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and Ottoman imperial orders had collapsed or been radically transformed. New states and mandates emerged, but self-determination was applied selectively, colonial rule continued, and millions remained minorities within new borders. The United States rejected League membership yet remained economically and diplomatically active; the unstable settlement shaped later conflict without predetermining it.
